title: Thevenin's Theorem Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 11
description:
Aarav has a circuit with a battery and two resistors, and five different loads to test. Must he solve the whole circuit five times? Network theorems are the shortcut. We meet superposition, Norton's theorem and maximum power transfer, then focus on the most used of all: Thevenin's theorem (Helmholtz 1853, Thévenin 1883). Any linear circuit, seen from two terminals A and B, acts like one voltage source in series with one resistance.

We find V_TH and R_TH in four steps (remove the load, measure the open-circuit voltage, short the battery and look in from A and B, rebuild the copy). On a live breadboard the real circuit and its Thevenin copy carry exactly the same load current, and the oscilloscope shows both load voltages moving together as a knob changes the load. Then the load-power curve peaks when R_L = R_TH, giving P_max = V_TH²/4R_TH. A worked example, the exam trap (short voltage sources, open current sources), where it is asked, an original JEE Main pattern practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 12 of PUC Electronics, Class 11, Chapter 2: Principles of Electricity, Network Theorems and AC Principles (Karnataka PUC Electronics).
